scope: Exact external crop/disease aliases with source-backed non-chemical reference steps. These entries do not verify that an image diagnosis is correct and do not provide chemical products or dosage.

entries.heading: Banana Sigatoka leaf-spot guidance
entries.message: These non-chemical steps are described by Kerala Agricultural University for Sigatoka leaf spot. A photo cannot confirm the pathogen; check with a local expert before disease-specific action.
steps: Remove severely infected and completely dried leaves, following local disposal guidance.
Maintain field drainage, suitable spacing, and weed control.
Confirm the exact leaf-spot disease locally; several banana conditions can look similar.

entries.heading: Banana leaf-spot references
entries.message: The assessment used a broad leaf-spot label, which does not identify a specific disease. These university pages describe Sigatoka types of leaf spot for comparison; they do not confirm that this is the condition in your photo.
steps: Compare the whole plant and lesion pattern with the linked disease descriptions; a close-up photo alone may not distinguish causes.
Keep a record of whether new spots are appearing or spreading.
Ask a local agricultural expert to identify the cause before choosing disease-specific control.

entries.heading: General banana leaf-spot guidance
entries.message: KAU's page is for Sigatoka leaf spot (Cercospora musae), while Black Sigatoka is a distinct disease. The steps below are general leaf-spot reference information, not a confirmed treatment for Black Sigatoka.
steps: Remove severely infected and completely dried leaves, following local disposal guidance.
Maintain field drainage and suitable plant spacing.
Ask a local expert to confirm the exact Sigatoka disease before selecting control measures.

entries.heading: Mango leaf-spot references
entries.message: The assessment used a broad leaf-spot label and did not identify a specific cause. Mango anthracnose and grey blight are two separate conditions described by KAU; these links are for comparison, not confirmation.
steps: Compare the shape, location, and progression of spots with the linked descriptions; do not assume they are the same disease.
Photograph the affected leaf and monitor whether new spots appear or existing spots enlarge.
Ask a local horticulture expert to confirm the cause before removing plant parts or choosing disease-specific control.

entries.heading: Mango anthracnose reference steps
entries.message: Kerala Agricultural University's page describes mango anthracnose symptoms and management. The image assessment cannot confirm the pathogen; these are general, non-chemical reference steps.
steps: Keep the canopy from becoming excessively dense; ask a local horticulture expert about suitable pruning timing.
Remove visibly affected fallen plant debris using locally appropriate disposal practices.
Have the diagnosis checked, especially if twigs, flowers, or fruit are also affected.

entries.heading: Mango powdery-mildew reference steps
entries.message: The linked KAU page describes mango powdery mildew, including white powdery growth on leaves and flowering parts. A photo cannot confirm the cause; this is general non-chemical reference information.
steps: Check whether powdery growth is present on leaves, flower stalks, flowers, or young fruit; confirm locally if unclear.
Maintain overall plant health and monitor new growth.
Ask a local horticulture expert to distinguish disease from dust, residue, or other leaf problems.

entries.heading: Mango grey-blight reference steps
entries.message: KAU describes grey blight as lesions that can begin at leaf margins or tips and enlarge. The assessment is preliminary; confirm the cause before removing plant material.
steps: Photograph affected leaves and monitor whether spots enlarge or spread to new growth.
If affected plant parts are removed, follow local expert advice on safe disposal.
Ask a local horticulture expert to confirm grey blight rather than another leaf disorder.

entries.heading: Chilli leaf-spot references
entries.message: The broad leaf-spot label does not identify a cause. Chilli anthracnose, bacterial leaf spot, and Cercospora leaf spot are different conditions; use these pages for comparison only and seek local confirmation.
steps: Compare lesion shape and progression against the source descriptions; leaf spots can have different causes.
Take clear photos of both sides of several affected leaves and monitor spread.
Ask a local agricultural expert to confirm the cause before choosing disease-specific control.

entries.heading: Chilli anthracnose reference steps
entries.message: KAU's chilli page describes anthracnose mainly on fruit, which may later be associated with leaf blight. The photo does not confirm that diagnosis; use these as general non-chemical practices.
steps: Use healthy, disease-free seed for future planting.
Avoid overhead watering where feasible to limit prolonged wetness on foliage and fruit.
Remove fallen infected debris using locally appropriate disposal practices and seek confirmation if symptoms spread.

entries.heading: Chilli bacterial-wilt reference steps
entries.message: Sudden persistent wilting can have multiple causes. KAU's page describes bacterial wilt signs and preventive field practices; get local confirmation before removing plants or taking disease-specific action.
steps: Check whether lower leaves wilt suddenly while the plant remains green; a local expert can inspect the stem for bacterial ooze.
For future planting, use healthy planting material and well-drained raised beds where suitable.
Avoid moving soil or plant material from a suspect area until you have local advice.

entries.heading: Chilli powdery-mildew reference steps
entries.message: KAU describes white powdery growth on chilli stems and leaves, often on lower leaves. A photograph cannot establish the cause; this is general reference guidance.
steps: Check the undersides and lower leaves for powdery growth and monitor whether it spreads.
Maintain field sanitation and remove fallen debris using local guidance.
Ask an agricultural expert to confirm the cause before applying any disease-specific control.
